newsitem.title: USA: U.S. markets find footing after sell-off.
newsitem.headline: U.S. markets find footing after sell-off.

text.p: Financial markets found their footing on Tuesday after remarks from Japan's prime minister sparked a sharp sell-off in the stock market late on Monday.
Stocks rose and bonds and the dollar also edged higher after investors were soothed by Japan's efforts at damage control following Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's remarks.
The Dow Jones industrial average, which fell to its second biggest point loss ever on Monday, rose 33.25 points to 7,637.51 at midday.

After a speech at Columbia University, Hashimoto said he would like the United States to help stabilise foreign exchange rates since currency swings might cause the Japanese government to sell U.S. government securities.
Stock prices tumbled as investors interpreted the comments as a veiled threat by Japan to sell off its U.S. Treasury bond holdings, which could cause havoc in U.S. markets.
The Dow tumbled 192.25 points, second only to the 508-point drop when the market crashed on Oct. 19, 1987.

But Japan quickly backpedaled from the remarks, with the country's finance minister saying Hashimoto's real intention was not correctly reported, and that Japan had no intention of selling U.S. Treasuries.
"The market was in a position to bounce back and the bounce should stick," said Dan Ascani, president and director of research at Global Market Strategists Inc.
While stocks recovered, the Dow gave back much of its gain of 80 points registered early in the session.
The 30-year Treasury bond was little changed, with its yield at 6.71 percent.
The dollar rose to 114.80 Japanese yen after dipping to 114.10 yen overnight, up slightly from 114.76 late on Monday in New York. It rose to 1.7255 German marks from 1.7175 late on Monday.
"We recovered pretty smartly," said Mike Malpede, a senior foreign exchange analyst at Refco Group Ltd. "Hashimoto's backpedalling and the Japanese are saying all the right things."
Market players said they did not think Hashimoto's remarks reflected any strategic shift in thinking by the Japanese.
Abby Joseph Cohen, co-chair of the investment policy committee at Goldman Sachs and Co., said she did not expect a significant change in Japanese participation in U.S. financial markets.

But Monday's selloff could be a sign of further volatility ahead, particularily in the high-flying stock market, analysts said. In Monday's sell-off, some investors used Hashimoto's remarks as an excuse to take profits, they said.
"We're trading at a rich valuation that doesn't give you much of a cushion should some kind of unexpected negative event hit," said Douglas Cliggott, U.S. equity strategist at J.P. Morgan.
Stock markets in Europe ended mostly higher, boosted by Wall Street's recovery.
Gold, which rallied on Hashimoto's remarks, pulled back. Gold for August delivery fell 30 cents to $340.80 an ounce on New York's Commodity Exchange.
